label: bm-clients-and-market
topic: Who would pay, and for what: buyers, partners and procurement routes for a law-constrained printable responsive material
summary: Who would pay, and for what: the evidence supports three payers and one gap. (1) Clients pay for finished installations: Mamou-Mani's pages name Hyundai Motor (through the artist's Tate Modern commission), Neko Health, COS, Hermes (via RDAI) and Buro Happold as sponsors or clients, and its fabrication arm Fab.Pub (a Therme Group joint venture) has a public material-intake route and a GBP 250 minimum budget, but no published fees. (2) Public funders pay for proof-of-concept research: NSF SBIR/STTR (Phase I ceiling USD 335,937 and Phase II USD 2,239,578 as of 16 Oct 2026; my sample of 118 NSF awards has medians near USD 305k and USD 1.25m), UK Knowledge Transfer Partnerships (GBP 8,500 per month of eligible cost, 12-36 months; round one of 2026-27 closed), and the Royce industrial collaboration programme. Innovate UK Smart grants, named in the brief, are closed. (3) Manufacturers take part rather than pay: Warema and Schueco were 'external partners' in a ministry-funded Fraunhofer ISE project, Fraunhofer ISE says manufacturers commission facility tests, and Schueco's start-up programme offers non-financial help. Gap: no firm was found that pays for a law-constrained material or verified rule as such; Foster + Partners and ZHA have in-house research and a 2017 Autodesk passive-facade study but no buying evidence. Formlabs offers Open Material Mode (from USD 875, free to accredited education), in-kind consumables for student groups and a certified-materials track, but no sponsored-research programme. Contradictions with earlier files: Open Material Mode price (store page 'from $875' vs a reseller listing of about USD 3.7k in bm-formlabs-printing-workflows.json); Smart grants closed; SBIR Phase I top is USD 335,937 on one sbir.gov page and USD 323,000 on another.
lay_summary: We looked for people who might pay for a printable material that follows proven rules. We found plenty of people who pay for finished installations, such as a car maker backing an art commission in a London gallery, a health clinic and a fashion brand. We found almost no one who pays for the material or the rule on its own. The likely first money is public: grants in the US and UK that pay universities and small companies to prove an idea. Big window and shade makers join those public projects but say they offer help, not cash. Think of it as selling a seed sample to a garden designer: she may plant it, but a research fund will pay for growing it.

findings.claim: Mamou-Mani's Tate Modern Turbine Hall piece (2025-26) was delivered inside an artist commission whose sponsor is Hyundai Motor; the practice is the architecture studio partner, so the payer of record is the artist/commission, not a materials buyer.
findings.evidence_quote: Hyundai Commission: Tarek Atoui is in partnership with Hyundai Motor

findings.claim: The same Tate project used an independent structural engineer (Webb Yates Engineers) for suspension and load tests of the printed parts, i.e. a consultancy is already in the verification chain for printed architectural pieces.
findings.evidence_quote: suspension and load tests carried out with Webb Yates Engineers verified the fixings before installation

findings.claim: Neko Health is the named client of the Monolith Wall (260 printed panels in recycled PETG per the earlier record); Fab.Pub, not the practice, is the producer.
findings.evidence_quote: Client Neko Health Collaborators Acrylicize

findings.claim: COS is the named client of Conifera, the 700-module PLA pavilion (Milan 2019); the project is a brand-funded installation.
findings.evidence_quote: Client COS FabPub Ltd

findings.claim: Hermes is the named client of the Beijing Sanlitun facade, done by RDAI in collaboration with Mamou-Mani: a luxury retail client buying a facade through a lead architect, with Mamou-Mani as sub-consultant.
findings.evidence_quote: Client: Hermès Architects for the building and interior: RDAI Architects for the facade: RDAI in collaboration with Mamou-Mani Architects

findings.claim: Buro Happold, an engineering consultancy, was the client for Mamou-Mani's Wooden Waves ceiling installation: an engineering firm has already commissioned this practice.
findings.evidence_quote: Client - Burohappold

findings.claim: Fab.Pub has a public material-intake route: a visitor is asked to send a material source, volume and intended application, and Fab.Pub then helps define a testing pathway. This is the most direct, documented door for offering a new material to this practice's fabrication arm.
findings.evidence_quote: Send us the material source, approximate volume and the product or application you have in mind.

findings.claim: Fab.Pub says its material work involves collaboration with researchers and industry to test formulations in real manufacturing conditions, so sponsored or joint testing (not just sales) is the stated mode.
findings.evidence_quote: Through collaboration with researchers and industry, we test how new formulations behave in real manufacturing conditions

findings.claim: Fab.Pub's quote form states a minimum budget of GBP 250 and the home page a minimum 2-week lead time; no price list or day rate for commissions was found on any page read.
findings.evidence_quote: Total Budget (Minimum Budget: £250)

findings.claim: Fab.Pub offers franchise and joint-venture arrangements built around buying Mobile Factories; the investment amount is not published.
findings.evidence_quote: The Fab.Pub franchise model involves an initial investment in Mobile Factories

findings.claim: Fab.Pub is a joint venture between Therme Group and Mamou-Mani Architects (Therme's own blog), so a larger corporate backer sits behind the fabrication arm.
findings.evidence_quote: FabPub (Fabrication Public) is a joint venture between Therme Group and Mamou-Mani Architects.

findings.claim: The practice sells 'parametric consultancy' as a service (geometry adapted to environmental constraints), which is the closest existing service line to a law-constrained design tool.
findings.evidence_quote: Parametric Consultancy Our team uses parametric software to create complex geometries that adapt to environmental constraints.

findings.claim: Foster + Partners' Applied Research + Development group reports a 2017 collaboration with Autodesk on predicting how a passively actuated facade responds to temperature change: direct evidence that a major practice spends effort on exactly this class of material behaviour. No evidence was found that they buy materials or fund outside labs for it.
findings.evidence_quote: In collaboration with Autodesk in 2017, we used Machine Learning to predict how a passively actuated façade would react to temperature change.

findings.claim: Foster + Partners states it does research and development with universities and industry partners (page dated 2020 by AECbytes).
findings.evidence_quote: We conduct state-of-the-art research and development in collaboration with universities and industry partners

findings.claim: Zaha Hadid Architects has an in-house research group (ZHA CODE) founded in 2007 per its history page; a 2018 press listing named Stratasys and the Block Research Group among collaborators (search summary, not fetched), so ZHA is a candidate collaborator rather than a documented customer.
findings.evidence_quote: We established our first formal research group, ZHA’s Computation and Design Group (ZHA CODE), pioneering new technologies for design and construction.

findings.claim: ZHA CODE is described as a practice-embedded research group, i.e. R&D is inside the firm; any engagement would be a collaboration or pilot, not a purchase.
findings.evidence_quote: a practice-embedded group that bridges research with practical architectural applications

findings.claim: Arup has long-running strategic research partnerships with universities (Cambridge for more than 60 years; Manchester announced in 2023 with materials named as a research area). Arup is therefore reachable through a university sponsored-research agreement; no Arup page read states that it buys outside material R&D directly.
findings.evidence_quote: Arup and Cambridge have been working together for more than 60 years

findings.claim: The Manchester-Arup strategic partnership names materials among its research areas.
findings.evidence_quote: collaborative research initiatives will delve into advancements in materials, social design methodologies, data science

findings.claim: A New Zealand research project lists Buro Happold and BioMat as international collaborators on scalable shading prototypes using biomaterial-based and 4D-printed components (project page, undated, preliminary).
findings.evidence_quote: International collaborators, including BioMat and Buro Happold, contribute global expertise to the development of scalable shading prototypes.

findings.claim: Schueco runs a start-up programme (GrowthFactory) aimed at start-ups that complement its building-envelope business; a responsive facade material would fit this stated scope.
findings.evidence_quote: Your Start-up complements our core business around intelligent building envelopes

findings.claim: Schueco's page says it offers start-ups non-financial resources (market access, know-how) rather than large budgets. The evidence therefore supports a pilot or co-development engagement, not a paid purchase.
findings.evidence_quote: for Start-ups, it’s not always just about securing big budgets. Sometimes it’s about gaining access to non-financial resources.

findings.claim: Schueco's 2025 turnover was EUR 2.06 billion with 6,750 employees (company press page), so it is large enough to fund a pilot but nothing read shows it paying a start-up for material R&D.
findings.evidence_quote: In 2025, Schüco achieved a turnover of €2.06 billion with 6750 employees.

findings.claim: WAREMA (sun shading) and Schueco both took part as 'external partners' in the publicly funded Synergy Facade project led by Fraunhofer ISE (2021-2024). Manufacturers join publicly funded research rather than commissioning it alone.
findings.evidence_quote: Project Partners: Priedemann Facade-Lab, Transsolar Energietechnik, Warema (external partner), Schüco (external partner)

findings.claim: The Synergy Facade project was sponsored by the German federal economics and climate ministry.
findings.evidence_quote: Contracting Authority/ Sponsors: Federal Ministry for Economic Affairs and Climate Action

findings.claim: Fraunhofer ISE says characterisation in its CONTINENT outdoor facility is commissioned by facade-technology manufacturers: a fee-for-service route by which a manufacturer would have third-party comfort and energy data on a new shading material.
findings.evidence_quote: characterization is also commissioned by manufacturers of facade technology

findings.claim: WAREMA Group revenue was about EUR 687 million in 2024 (EUR 753 million in 2023), so it is a mid-size firm with falling sales in the latest year reported.
findings.evidence_quote: the company achieved a total revenue of around 687 million euros (2023: 753 million euros)

findings.claim: MIT's Self-Assembly Lab says it is supported annually by grants, gifts and sponsored research and invites companies to contact it about partnering: a documented sponsored-research door for programmable-material work.
findings.evidence_quote: The lab is generously supported annually by grants, gifts and sponsored research.

findings.claim: The lab's 4D printing programme was a collaboration with Stratasys and Autodesk, i.e. industry has funded or supplied printers for this field before.
findings.evidence_quote: 4D Printing, developed as a collaboration between the Self-Assembly Lab, Stratasys and Autodesk

findings.claim: The University of Stuttgart's ICD ran a 2021-22 project on zero-energy self-shading, funded by a university-internal knowledge and technology transfer scheme. ICD is both a likely academic partner and a competitor for the same public funds.

findings.evidence_quote: As of October 16, 2026, agencies may issue a Phase I award (including modifications) up to $335,937 and a Phase II award (including modifications) up to $2,239,578 without seeking SBA approval.

findings.claim: The same site's 'apply' page gives older ranges: Phase I USD 50,000-323,000 and Phase II USD 650,000-2.2 million. Two pages on one site disagree (323,000 vs 335,937 is 12,937 USD, 3.8 percent, my arithmetic); the 'about' page is dated.
findings.evidence_quote: Award Amounts: $50,000-$323,000

findings.claim: Phase II range on the apply page.
findings.evidence_quote: Award Amounts: $650,000-$2.2 million

findings.claim: SBIR eligibility: a for-profit US company with under 500 employees, owned and controlled by US citizens or permanent residents. A university or non-profit cannot receive the SBIR award directly.
findings.evidence_quote: Is a for-profit entity located in the U.S. Has fewer than 500 employees (most applicants have fewer than 10). Is owned and controlled by U.S. citizens or permanent residents.

findings.claim: STTR requires the small business to formally partner with a research institution, which suits a university-plus-company team.
findings.evidence_quote: The primary difference from SBIR is that for STTR, the small business must formally partner with a research institution.

findings.claim: Each agency may add up to USD 6,500 per year (Phase I) and USD 50,000 per award (Phase II) for technical and business assistance on top of the award.
findings.evidence_quote: up to $6,500 per year for Phase I awards and up to $50,000 per award for Phase II awards

findings.claim: Own calculation on 118 distinct NSF award records returned by my keyword queries (script nsf_stats.py): median SBIR Phase I = USD 304,990 (n=20), median STTR Phase I = USD 305,000 (n=15), median SBIR Phase II = USD 1,246,061 (n=35), I-Corps = USD 50,000 (n=43). Keyword searches were noisy so this is a sample of NSF award sizes, not all awards.
findings.value: NSF Phase I ~USD 305k; Phase II ~USD 1.25m; I-Corps USD 50k

findings.claim: Innovate UK Smart grants are closed to new applications (UKRI guidance page). The task brief lists them as a route; they are not available now.
findings.evidence_quote: Smart grants are now closed for new applications as funding is being aligned to Innovate UK’s new strategic direction

findings.claim: A secondary source (Grantsights, 29 Oct 2026) says UKRI's replacement, Velocity, launches in autumn 2027 and will carry all Innovate UK support. I could not confirm the Velocity date on a UKRI page.
findings.evidence_quote: Velocity will launch in autumn 2027 and that all Innovate UK support will be offered through it from then on

findings.claim: Knowledge Transfer Partnerships: academic institutions, RTOs or Catapults lead with a UK business; round one of 2026-27 had a fund of up to GBP 10 million and is closed (listing status Closed). Later 2026-27 rounds were reported by an aggregator but I did not confirm their dates.
findings.evidence_quote: can apply for a share of up to £10 million to fund innovation projects with businesses

findings.claim: KTP round-one listing status.
findings.evidence_quote: Opportunity status: Closed

findings.claim: KTP projects run 12-36 months at about GBP 8,500 of eligible cost per month; Innovate UK pays a proportion and the business partner pays the rest. My arithmetic: 8,500 x 12 = GBP 102,000 to 8,500 x 36 = GBP 306,000 total eligible cost per project.
findings.evidence_quote: Projects must be between 12 and 36 months. A project’s total eligible costs are typically £8,500 per month. A proportion of the eligible costs will be funded by Innovate UK, the remainder are paid by the business partner.

findings.claim: The Henry Royce Institute's Industrial Collaboration Programme funds industry-led, academic-engaged advanced-materials projects; Leeds won over GBP 300,000 in round six (21 Jul 2026), showing that the scheme is live. Eligibility and per-project size were not read.
findings.evidence_quote: The University of Leeds has secured over £300,000 funding from round six of the Henry Royce Institute’s Industrial Collaboration Programme (ICP), designed to support industry-led, academic engaged projects that address national advanced materials challenges.

findings.claim: AIA's Upjohn Research Initiative gave USD 100,000 across four architecture research projects in 2018 (the only year read), so it is a small, practitioner-facing funder; its current status is not confirmed.
findings.evidence_quote: The jury for the American Institute of Architects (AIA) Upjohn Research Initiative is providing $100,000 in grants to four research projects

findings.claim: The UK Lambert Toolkit provides model university-business collaboration agreements, including a contract-research model in which the university may not publish without the sponsor's permission; the guidance says it was last updated in 2018.
findings.evidence_quote: Agreement 5 Contract research: no publication by Institution without Collaborator’s permission

findings.claim: Lambert guidance age.
findings.evidence_quote: This guidance was last updated in 2018

findings.claim: I found no firm that documents paying an outside party for a law-constrained or verified material or design rule as such. Documented payers are (1) clients buying finished installations (Hyundai/Tate, Neko Health, COS, Hermes, Buro Happold), (2) public funders, and (3) manufacturers who join publicly funded projects or buy test time. Absence of evidence in the pages read, not proof of absence.
findings.source: synthesis of the findings above; pages saved under data/bm-clients-market/ and data/mamou-mani/

Confirms the earlier spec-ip-landscape caution that sponsor rights and IP position matter before any sponsored-research or SBIR work: nothing here changes that file's finding that stimulus-responsive printed objects are a crowded patent field.
findings.evidence_quote: Smart grants are now closed for new applications as funding is being aligned to Innovate UK’s new strategic direction

findings.claim: Deepens bm-passive-facades-evidence.json (no measured building benefit for humidity-driven shading; no commercial product found): this run also found no start-up or product selling a humidity-driven printed shading element. The documented academic work is public-funded (the Nature Communications 2024 paper lists Deutsche Forschungsgemeinschaft as funder in Crossref), which points to public grants, not market sales, as the first money.

key_claims.claim: Innovate UK Smart grants, which the brief lists, are closed to new applications; Knowledge Transfer Partnerships, SBIR/STTR and the Royce ICP are the live routes read in this run.
key_claims.evidence_quote: Smart grants are now closed for new applications as funding is being aligned to Innovate UK’s new strategic direction

key_claims.claim: SBIR needs a US-owned for-profit company; a university-and-company team would use STTR, which requires a formal research-institution partner. Phase I ceiling USD 335,937 and Phase II USD 2,239,578 as of 16 Oct 2026 (the apply page still shows the older USD 323,000 Phase I top).
key_claims.evidence_quote: As of October 16, 2026, agencies may issue a Phase I award (including modifications) up to $335,937 and a Phase II award (including modifications) up to $2,239,578 without seeking SBA approval.

key_claims.claim: The practice's documented clients pay for finished installations (Hyundai Motor via the Tate commission, Neko Health, COS, Buro Happold), and Fab.Pub has an explicit door for new materials (send material source, volume, application) with a GBP 250 minimum job budget; no commission fees are published.
key_claims.evidence_quote: Send us the material source, approximate volume and the product or application you have in mind.

key_claims.claim: No evidence was found that any facade manufacturer or Formlabs pays outsiders for new material R&D: Schueco says it offers start-ups non-financial resources, and Formlabs offers in-kind consumables and certification, not research money.
key_claims.evidence_quote: for Start-ups, it’s not always just about securing big budgets. Sometimes it’s about gaining access to non-financial resources.

recommendations: Treat the proof of concept as a sample plus a verified design rule, not a product. Nothing read shows anyone paying for a rule as such; the documented money is installation fees, public grants and test fees. The project record's thin-bilayer limit (about 0.2-0.9 mm total thickness for stock-resin humidity actuation, bm-passive-facades-evidence.json) points to interior, installation and demonstrator uses first, not full-scale shading.

Approach Fab.Pub through its public material-intake route with a hand-scale sample, a one-page rule sheet (the 3/2 ceiling and what it permits) and a request for a joint test pathway. Ask Mamou-Mani what a paid prototype or joint pilot would cost, since no fee is published.

Choose the money route by who the applicant is. US for-profit: NSF Project Pitch under Advanced Materials sub-topic 5 (Structural and Infrastructural Materials), roughly USD 305k Phase I; check the current solicitation and deadline on seedfund.nsf.gov. Team with a university: STTR. UK company plus university: a KTP in a later round (round-one 2026-27 closed) or Royce ICP. Smart grants are not available.

For a UK university-company deal use a Lambert Toolkit agreement as a starting point; the contract-research model lets the sponsor control publication. Settle background IP first, since the earlier IP scan found the responsive-printed-object field crowded.
To get manufacturer evidence without selling to them, price a Fraunhofer ISE CONTINENT characterisation request, or join a publicly funded consortium as Warema and Schueco did.

Do not plan on Formlabs money. Ask for in-kind resin only if a student or accredited academic partner is the applicant, and use free Open Material Mode through an educational partner if a non-Formlabs resin is needed.

could_not_find: Any published fee, day rate or commission value for Mamou-Mani or Fab.Pub beyond the GBP 250 minimum job budget; their franchise investment amount is also unpublished.

Any page showing Foster + Partners, ZHA, Arup or Buro Happold buying external material research (only collaborations and in-house groups). Foster's own page URLs returned HTTP 403 to my fetch; I used an AECbytes feature (2020) instead.

Any facade or shading maker (Schueco, WAREMA, Hunter Douglas, Permasteelisa, Colt) that pays a start-up or university for material R&D. Hunter Douglas, Permasteelisa and Colt: a search found no university research collaboration and I did not fetch their sites.
Any start-up or product selling a humidity-driven printed shading or cladding element (a web search returned only academic projects).
A market-size figure for responsive or passive shading; I found only two company revenue figures (Schueco, WAREMA) and did not use any analyst figure.
Whether the team is a US for-profit company, a UK company, or a university group; this decides SBIR vs STTR vs KTP and I did not guess.
Current NSF Project Pitch status and next full-proposal deadline: aggregator pages disagree (one says March 4, 2027; another says pitches were paused) and I did not read the NSF solicitation text.
KTP round dates after round one of 2026-27 (aggregators gave Round 2 and 3 dates; unverified here) and the grant percentage by business size (garbled in the search snippet).
Royce ICP eligibility and per-project size; the Leeds page gives only a total across projects (over GBP 300,000).

Formlabs: any sponsored-research, materials-partner or architecture-practice programme; the Form 4 Open Material Mode price (the page shows only 'From $875' for six SKUs); the full list of Certified Materials. Formlabs' Developer Platform page returned 404.
Whether anyone would pay for the Lean-checked rule itself. No source was found; this is a market-test question for the team.
Procurement timelines (how long a sponsored research agreement or SBIR award takes to sign). Not researched.
MIT Self-Assembly Lab sponsor list and fee levels; the partners page gave no names or amounts.
Arup Global Research Challenge details: only a 2017 trade-press article was read and it is not used for any claim.

glossary.plain: US government grants that pay small companies (STTR: together with a university) to test a new technology.
The first small grant to prove an idea, then a larger one to build it.
A UK scheme in which a university and a company share the cost of a project that places a graduate in the company.
A contract in which a company pays a university to do research, and the contract sets who owns the results.
Template contracts from the UK government for university-business research deals.
A paid unlock that lets a Formlabs printer use resin or powder made by other companies.
The outer skin of a building.
A firm that sells engineering advice and checks, such as testing that a hanging part is safe.
Money that does not require giving up a share of the company.
Goods such as resin given instead of cash.
